name: Cybersecurity for AI Devices
blurb: The FDA's premarket cybersecurity expectations as they apply to AI.
title: Cybersecurity for AI Devices
answer: Connected and AI enabled devices must show cybersecurity risk management in their premarket submissions, including a software bill of materials and plans for patching. AI adds its own attack surface, from poisoned training data to manipulated inputs, which should be part of the same threat model.

reading.body:
The FDA treats cybersecurity as premarket content for connected and AI enabled devices, not a post-market afterthought.

The expectation is concrete: cybersecurity risk management in the submission, a software bill of materials, and a plan for patching. Those are documentation and process requirements, and they apply before a device reaches a patient rather than after a vulnerability is found.

AI changes the threat model that documentation has to cover. Poisoned training data, manipulated inputs and model theft sit alongside the conventional device attack surface, and the data's guidance is to add them from the start rather than bolt them on. For a medtech team this is a scoping decision made early, when the threat model is written, because a submission built around network security alone will not describe the model specific risks.

What this does not cover is the substance of the guidance itself. There is one dated development, the 2023 FDA cybersecurity guidance, and no detail on submission formats, review timelines, or how any of it has been enforced. It also says nothing about compute, buildings or power, so no claim about infrastructure can be drawn from it.

explainer:
Connected devices can be attacked like any other computer, and a compromised medical device can harm patients. US law requires makers of cyber devices to include cybersecurity information in premarket submissions, and the FDA's guidance describes what to provide: a threat model, cybersecurity risk assessment, a software bill of materials listing components, security testing results, and plans to monitor and patch vulnerabilities after launch.

AI adds threats specific to models. Training data can be poisoned to plant hidden behaviour, inputs can be crafted to fool a model, models can be extracted or inverted to reveal training data, and models that call other services expand the attack surface. Including these in the same threat model as conventional software threats, and testing for them, is the practical way to meet the FDA's expectations for AI enabled devices.

Why AI devices widen the attack surface

A connected medical device already has to defend against software vulnerabilities, network attacks and tampering. An AI device adds new targets. Its model can be manipulated through crafted inputs that cause wrong outputs, a technique known as an adversarial attack. Its training data and update channel can be poisoned so that a corrupted model is installed as if it were legitimate. And models that call cloud services send patient data over networks that must be protected. Regulators now treat cybersecurity as part of device safety, not an IT matter.

What regulators require

The FDA requires premarket submissions for cyber devices to include a security plan, a software bill of materials listing every component, evidence of secure design, and a plan for monitoring and patching vulnerabilities after release. European device rules and the EU AI Act add their own requirements on robustness and security. For AI specifically, manufacturers are expected to consider attacks on the model itself, to protect the integrity of updates, and to show that a model cannot be driven into unsafe outputs by inputs an attacker could supply.

The practical programme

Manufacturers run threat modelling that includes the model and its data pipeline, sign and verify every model update, restrict and monitor what the device sends to the cloud, test models against adversarial inputs, and keep a vulnerability disclosure process that covers AI components. Hospitals, for their part, ask for the bill of materials and the update policy before buying. The field is young, and the first disclosed vulnerabilities specific to medical AI are now appearing, which is why the monitoring and patching plan is where regulators look hardest.
